summary: Kingston, Pennsylvania, farmer and father of the nurse Catherine Scott Pringle; John's 4th-great-grandfather.
bio:
Stephen J. Scott was a farmer at Kingston in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania. The records disagree about his age and origin. The 1850 census of Kingston Township lists him as a 44-year-old farmer born in Pennsylvania, with his wife Julia Ann, 41, also born in Pennsylvania, and children Henry, 21, Catharine, 14, Hannah, 10, Caroline, 9, and Ann, 4; the 1880 census likewise gives Catherine's parents as Pennsylvania-born. A county history of 1893, however, says that Stephen and Julia Ann were both born in Connecticut, married there and moved to Kingston about 1818, and Catherine herself told the 1910 census that both her parents were born in Connecticut. The likeliest reading is that Stephen was born in Pennsylvania about 1806 and that the family's Connecticut roots belong to the generation before him, which would fit the Susquehanna Company settlers of the Wyoming Valley. His Kingston neighbours in 1850 included Zeba Hoyt, a Connecticut-born farmer of 61, German miners named Shoup, Steinhower and Beck, and Welsh miners and a machinist named Davis.

His parentage is not proven. Family trees name his parents as Daniel Scott and Hannah Devens, and there is some circumstantial support: Hannah Devens, a daughter of Leonard Devens, was baptized at the Walpack Dutch Reformed Church in Sussex County, New Jersey, in 1787; a Leonard Devens of Plymouth Township left a will registered in 1839, and Elizabeth Devens, 'wife of Leonard', died on 30 January 1858 aged 80 and was buried in the Shupp Cemetery at Larksville, so a Devens family was living in Plymouth Township in Stephen's lifetime. In 1810 a 'Daniel Scott Jr.' headed a household in Pittston Township that fits a couple with a son born in 1806 and a wife born about 1787, though the census names no one but the head. A speculative lead is that a Stephen Scott was one of 14 workmen who on 30 October 1818 refused to keep working on the Wilkes-Barre to Kingston bridge unless they were paid 'in good chartered notes', described as 'the first strike which the records of Wyoming disclose'; a Stephen Scott in Falls Township in 1840 was probably a different man.

Stephen died at Kingston on 19 April 1856, though the 1893 county history says 1855, and was buried in Forty Fort Cemetery. By July 1860 Julia Ann was a widow living in Plymouth Township with her youngest daughter Ann. He is John's 4th-great-grandfather, through his daughter Catherine Scott Pringle, the nurse.

researchNotes:
Stephen Scott was a farmer at Kingston. Sources conflict on his age and origin. The tree shows 1808-1856 (as an unaccepted 'Potential' hint). Bradsby (1893) says he and Julia Ann were both born in Connecticut, married there and moved to Kingston 'about 1818', and that he died in 1855; Round 1 therefore proposed a birth c.1797 or earlier. Round 3 reversed this: the 1850 census of Kingston Twp (3 Aug 1850, dwelling 262) lists Stephen Scott 44, farmer, b. Pa.; Julia Ann 41, b. Pa.; Henry 21; Catharine 14; Hannah 10; Caroline 9; Ann 4, and the 1880 census also gives Catherine's parents as born in Pennsylvania. Preferred: born c.1806 in Pennsylvania (any Connecticut roots belong a generation earlier, fitting the Susquehanna Company settlers of Wyoming Valley). FamilySearch gives his death as 19 Apr 1856 at Kingston, with burial in Forty Fort Cemetery (Bradsby: 1855). His Kingston neighbours in 1850 included Zeba Hoyt (61, CT-born farmer), German miners (Shoup, Steinhower, Beck) and Welsh miners and a machinist (Davis). A FamilySearch father 'Daniel Scott 1788-1811' is only 18 years older and unsupported. Lead (speculative): a Stephen Scott was one of 14 workmen who on 30 Oct 1818 refused to keep working on the Wilkes-Barre-Kingston bridge unless paid 'in good chartered notes' - 'the first strike which the records of Wyoming disclose' (Harvey & Smith vol. IV). A Stephen Scott in Falls Twp in the 1840 index is probably a different man.

No record of Stephen's own parentage was found, but three new pieces of evidence bear on it. (1) The FamilySearch tree names his parents as Daniel Scott and Hannah Devens (no sources attached to the link) ([R4-S2]). Hannah Devens, daughter of Leendert (Leonard) Devens, was baptized at the Walpack Dutch Reformed Church, Sussex Co., New Jersey, in 1787 (FamilySearch index, [R4-S3]). A Leonard Devens of Plymouth Twp left a will registered in 1839 (Luzerne Will Book B p.20) ([R4-S4]), and Elizabeth Devens, 'wife of Leonard', died 30 Jan 1858 aged 80 and was buried in the Shupp Cemetery at Larksville, Plymouth Twp ([R4-S5]). So a Devens family was in Plymouth Twp in Stephen's lifetime, which makes the Devens link worth testing. (2) In 1810 a 'Daniel Scott Jr.' headed a household in Pittston Twp, Luzerne Co.: one man aged 26-44, one woman 16-25 and three children under 10, two of them boys ([R4-S6]). That fits a couple with a son born in 1806 and a wife born about 1787, though it does not name anyone. (3) Against a Pennsylvania birth, his daughter Catherine told the 1910 census that both her parents were born in Connecticut ([R4-S7]), as Bradsby said in 1893; the 1850 census says Pennsylvania. The Connecticut statement could reflect the family's Connecticut (Susquehanna Company) background rather than Stephen's own birthplace.

Julia Ann was a widow in July 1860, living in Plymouth Twp with her youngest daughter Ann ([R4-S1]). No will or estate entry for Stephen appears in the Luzerne wills index ([R4-S4]).
